summary.text: Michaelis–Menten kinetics is the model often assumed for enzyme reactions that involve a single substrate.
At low substrate concentration the rate rises in step with it, but at high concentration it levels off toward a limiting rate called Vₘₐₓ.
Kₘ is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of Vₘₐₓ, and the same model also describes things like protein–protein interaction.

facts.value: Substrate concentration giving half the maximum rate

items.prompt: A cook adds a tiny pinch of substrate to plenty of enzyme, then doubles the pinch. What happens to the reaction rate?

options.label: It stays the same, since the enzyme is already maxed out
It falls to half, as the enzyme gets crowded
It roughly doubles, rising in step with the substrate
It drops to zero, as the substrate swamps the enzyme

items.explain: At low substrate concentration the rate varies linearly with substrate concentration.

items.prompt: At very high substrate levels, adding even more barely changes the rate. Why?

options.label: Almost every enzyme molecule is already bound to substrate
The substrate has run out of energy
The enzyme concentration drops as substrate rises
The Kₘ shifts to match the substrate

items.explain: At high substrate the rate approaches a limit at which all enzyme molecules are bound to substrate, so the enzyme is saturated.

items.prompt: Two labs measure Kₘ for the same enzyme and substrate at the same temperature and pH, but one uses twice as much enzyme. What do they expect?

options.label: Twice the Kₘ in the richer lab
Half the Kₘ in the richer lab
No Kₘ, since more enzyme hides it
The same Kₘ in both labs

items.explain: Kₘ is not affected by the concentration of an enzyme; it depends on the enzyme, the substrate, and conditions like temperature and pH.

items.prompt: A lab doubles the amount of enzyme in a reaction with plenty of substrate. What happens to the limiting rate?

options.label: It halves, since the enzyme gets crowded
It doubles, since the limit scales with enzyme
It stays put, since only Kₘ matters
It drops to zero once saturated

items.explain: The limiting rate Vₘₐₓ equals k_cat times the enzyme concentration, so it scales with the amount of enzyme.

items.prompt: Henri first derived the equation but never applied it. What did Michaelis and Menten realise that made the work more productive?

options.label: That initial rates are simpler to analyse than a whole time course
That substrate concentration must always be plotted on a log scale
That Kₘ is always exactly equal to the dissociation constant
That only reactions with a single substrate can ever be measured

items.explain: Michaelis and Menten realized that analysing initial rates is simpler and more productive than following the whole time course, as Henri had tried.

items.prompt: A lab wants one number for how efficiently an enzyme turns a substrate into product. Which should they use?

Kₘ divided by k_cat
Vₘₐₓ on its own

paragraphs.heading: A model for enzyme speed
paragraphs.text: Michaelis–Menten kinetics is a model for the speed of reactions in which an enzyme turns a substrate, the molecule it acts on, into a product. It is often assumed for reactions with a single substrate, sometimes without checking whether the model's assumptions hold. Few enzyme reactions truly have just one substrate. Even so, the equation often still works when only one substrate's concentration is changed.

paragraphs.heading: Binding, then making product
paragraphs.text: The model pictures the substrate A joining the enzyme to form a combined unit called the enzyme-substrate complex, EA. This joining can run both ways, so the complex may fall apart again. Or it can go forward, one way only, to release the product P. Each step has its own rate constant: k₊₁ for binding, k₋₁ for coming apart, and k_cat for making product.

paragraphs.heading: From rising to levelling off
paragraphs.text: When there is little substrate, the rate climbs in direct step with the substrate concentration. When there is a lot, adding more barely matters, and the rate creeps toward a limit called Vₘₐₓ. That limit would mean every enzyme molecule is holding a substrate, and it is never quite reached. At that point the enzyme is said to be saturated. The number k_cat, called the turnover number, tells how many substrate molecules one enzyme molecule can convert per unit of time at most.

paragraphs.heading: What Kₘ tells you
paragraphs.text: The Michaelis constant, Kₘ, has units of concentration: it is the substrate concentration at which the rate reaches half its limit. It does not change with how much enzyme there is or how pure it is. It does depend on which enzyme and which substrate are involved, and on conditions such as temperature and pH. A related number, k_cat/Kₘ, called the specificity constant, measures how efficiently an enzyme turns substrate into product. Fumarase is one of the enzymes that reach the highest value theory allows, held back by how fast substrate can diffuse into the active site.

paragraphs.heading: Who really found it
paragraphs.text: The equation actually began with Henri, so a more accurate name is the Henri–Michaelis–Menten equation. Henri derived it but never tried to use it. Michaelis and Menten saw that studying the starting rates of reactions was simpler and more useful than following a reaction over time, as Henri had tried. They also knew that buffers were needed to hold the pH steady, which Henri did not.

paragraphs.heading: Plotting on a log scale
paragraphs.text: Michaelis and Menten did not plot the rate against plain substrate concentration, the usual way today. They plotted it against the logarithm of the concentration. That kind of plot is rarely used today to find Vₘₐₓ and Kₘ, but it is handy for comparing enzymes across a wide range of concentrations. The four mammalian forms of hexokinase, for example, are half-saturated by glucose at levels from about 0.02 mM to about 50 mM, a 2500-fold spread that a log plot can show on one graph.

paragraphs.heading: Uses beyond enzymes
paragraphs.text: The same model describes other kinds of biochemical binding, such as an antibody grabbing an antigen or two proteins sticking together. Applied to the growth of microbes, an equation of this shape is sometimes called the Monod equation. It has also been used for topics far from enzymes, from how the body clears alcohol from the blood to how limiting nutrients affect the growth of phytoplankton in the ocean.
